title: Why Connection Matters
hook: Strong relationships aren't just nice to have — they predict how long and how well you live, on par with diet and exercise.
key_points: Social connection is a core health factor, not just an emotional luxury.
Strong relationships are linked to longer life and lower risk of disease.
The U.S. Surgeon General calls connection a public health priority.
Small, regular contact with others counts — quality matters more than size of your circle.
content_html: We treat eating well and moving more as health behaviors, but tend to file friendship under "lifestyle." The U.S. Surgeon General argues that's a mistake: the strength of our relationships shapes our health as powerfully as the choices we make about food and exercise.
extra_html: According to the Surgeon General's work on social connection, people with strong relationships tend to live longer and have lower rates of serious illness, while people who are isolated face higher risks. That's why connection is now treated as a public health priority rather than a personal preference. The reassuring part is that you don't need a huge social circle — consistent, genuine contact with a few people matters more than the number. A standing call with a friend, a chat with a neighbor, or showing up for a group you care about all count. If isolation is weighing on your mood or health, it's worth raising with a clinician; this isn't a substitute for medical advice.

related.title: Loneliness Is a Health Risk
related.hook: Chronic loneliness isn't just a bad feeling — it's linked to higher risk of heart disease, depression, and early death. And it's far more common than people admit.

related.title: Building Everyday Resilience
related.hook: Resilience isn't a personality you're born with — it's a set of habits and connections you can build, the way you build a muscle.

related.title: What Mental Health Really Means
related.hook: Mental health isn't just the absence of illness — it's being able to cope with life's stresses, work, learn, and contribute. Everyone has it, and it can be cared for.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the U.S. Surgeon General treat social connection as a health issue, not just a social one?
flashcards.back_html: Because strong relationships are linked to longer life and lower risk of disease, while weak connection raises health risks — making connection a health factor comparable to diet and exercise.

flashcards.prompt: According to the Surgeon General, social connection is best described as:

choices.text: A foundational factor for physical and mental health
Important only for people who already feel lonely
A matter of personality with no health impact

flashcards.explanation_html: The Surgeon General frames connection as a public health priority that shapes both physical and mental health across the population.
